content: The treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) requires prolonged use of second-line anti-tuberculosis drugs. However, the regimens used for these conditions vary significantly. The World Health Organization (WHO) 2011 guidelines recommended that MDR-TB treatment should include, at a minimum, pyrazinamide, one second-line injectable drug (such as kanamycin, amikacin, or capreomycin), one later-generation fluoroquinolone (such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin), and at least two Group 4 drugs (such as ethionamide/prothionamide, cycloserine/terizidone, or para-aminosalicylic acid). A systematic review was conducted to update the evidence for MDR-TB treatment to inform the WHO Guideline Development Group. The review focused on the efficacy and safety of available drugs for treating MDR-TB patients. The drugs analyzed included first-line drugs (pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and high-dose isoniazid), injectable drugs (streptomycin, kanamycin, amikacin, and capreomycin), fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin), Group 4 drugs (ethionamide/prothionamide, cycloserine/terizidone, and para-aminosalicylic acid), and the new drug bedaquiline. Drugs from Group 5 were excluded from the review due to the availability of at least four independent systematic reviews on these drugs. The literature search was conducted using three major databases: MEDLINE, EMBASE, and The Cochrane Library. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Heading (MeSH) terms and free-text words related to MDR-TB, XDR-TB, drugs of interest, and treatment outcomes. The search was limited to studies published between January 2009 and August 2015, as previous reviews had already included studies up to December 2008. Two independent reviewers screened titles, abstracts, and full texts, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Studies were included if they met specific criteria, such as confirmed MDR-TB diagnosis, pulmonary TB, a minimum of 25 MDR-TB or XDR-TB patients treated, a clear treatment regimen, and reported outcomes such as end-of-treatment results, six-month culture conversion, or adverse events. Data from eligible studies were abstracted using a standardized form. Information collected included patient demographics, HIV status, prior TB treatment, drug susceptibility test results, treatment duration, and whether the regimen was standardized or individualized. Outcomes abstracted included end-of-treatment results, six-month sputum culture conversion, and serious adverse events (SAEs). SAEs were defined as Grade 3–4 events or events leading to permanent drug discontinuation. Statistical analyses were performed to pool data on treatment success rates and adverse events. The review identified 74 studies with 84 distinct cohorts, reporting on 17,494 MDR-TB and XDR-TB patients. Treatment success rates were significantly lower in XDR-TB patients (26%) compared to all MDR-TB cohorts (60%). Less than 3% of patients receiving fluoroquinolones or pyrazinamide experienced SAEs, while more than 5% of patients receiving second-line injectables or thioamides (ethionamide or prothionamide) experienced SAEs. Despite the large number of studies and patients, no specific treatment parameter, including the number or duration of drugs, was associated with improved six-month culture conversion or end-of-treatment outcomes. This may reflect limitations in data pooling rather than a true lack of differences in regimen efficacy. The review highlights the need for more standardized reporting and evidence from well-designed randomized trials or meta-analyses of pooled individual patient data from multiple observational studies. In children, MDR-TB is under-recognized, under-diagnosed, and under-reported. Approximately 32,000 children develop MDR-TB annually, yet optimal treatment strategies remain poorly understood. Treatment is challenging, requiring toxic medications for at least 18 months, often in formulations unsuitable for children. However, individual studies have reported successful treatment outcomes in at least 80% of children treated for MDR-TB. A systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis were conducted to address key questions regarding pediatric MDR-TB treatment and to inform pediatric-specific guidelines. Eligible datasets included those with at least three children (aged <15 years) treated for clinically or bacteriologically confirmed MDR-TB, with reported treatment outcomes. Both published and unpublished data were included, without date restrictions. Studies were excluded if they used only combinations of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, or streptomycin, as this is now considered inadequate therapy. Data were collected on demographic characteristics, nutritional status, HIV status, disease severity, drug susceptibility test results, and treatment regimens. Outcomes included cure, treatment completion, culture conversion by six months, treatment failure, relapse, loss to follow-up, and mortality. The review underscores the need for rigorous evidence to optimize treatment outcomes and minimize adverse events in children with MDR-TB.
